text: A medical emergency. The body’s core temperature rises above about 40 °C and its cooling system fails. Without fast cooling it can kill or cause lasting organ damage.

source.label: National Centre for Disease Control, India: heat-related illnesses

text: The warning stage before heatstroke: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness and nausea. Rest, water and cooling usually bring recovery.
When the body takes in or makes more heat than it can shed, from hot air, humidity, sun and physical work.

The point beyond which adjusting no longer prevents harm. Places used to heat cope better with days of 30–35 °C, but a study of 2.7 million firms found no adaptation to days above 40 °C. Cutting emissions keeps more places below that limit.

source.label: OECD Economics Department, Working Paper No. 1828, 2024

text: The body slowly adjusting to heat over one to two weeks. New and returning workers are most at risk until it has.
Deaths above the normal number for that place and time of year. Because death certificates rarely say “heat”, this is how the real toll of a heatwave is counted.

Heat and humidity combined into one number, read from a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth. It shows whether sweat can still cool you. A wet-bulb temperature of 35 °C is often quoted as the limit of human survival; recent studies suggest the real limit is lower.

source.label: Vecellio et al., Journal of Applied Physiology, 2022, summarised by Penn State

text: Dry heat is high temperature with low humidity: sweat still evaporates, but the body soaks up heat fast. It peaks in South Asia’s pre-monsoon months. Humid heat is warm, wet air in which sweat can’t evaporate, so the body can’t cool itself even at lower temperatures. It dominates Southeast Asia and builds through South Asia’s monsoon, and it is rising faster than dry heat. The two need different warnings and different cooling.

source.label: Ivanovich et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 2024

text: The workplace measure of heat. It adds sun and wind to heat and humidity, and is used to set rest breaks and stop work.
The “feels-like” temperature in the shade, combining air temperature and humidity. In the Philippines, a heat index of 42 °C or more is officially a danger level.

source.label: PAGASA: heat index

text: A spell of unusually hot weather for that place. There is no single global definition: each country sets its own thresholds.
Nights that stay too hot for the body to recover from the day. They are often more dangerous than hot days, and they are rising faster.
Cities running several degrees hotter than the countryside around them, especially at night, because of concrete, traffic, waste heat and few trees.
A city’s or country’s plan for the heat season: who issues warnings, at what temperature, and what hospitals, employers and services do next.
A forecast that reaches people in time, in a form they understand, with clear advice on what to do.
Acting on a forecast, before a disaster peaks, by releasing pre-agreed money and help when a trigger is reached.
A public place, such as a library, school or community hall, kept cool during heatwaves for people with no cool space at home.
Insurance that pays out automatically when a measured trigger, such as a temperature threshold, is crossed. There is no claim form and no damage assessment.
When the trigger and the real loss don’t match: people suffer from the heat, but the threshold isn’t crossed and no payout comes.
A group of countries, cities or insurers that share the cost of disasters, so no single member carries a catastrophe alone.
Public support such as pensions, cash transfers and unemployment benefits that keeps households out of poverty when income stops.
Cooling a building without using power: shade, airflow, insulation, orientation and reflective surfaces.
A roof painted or built to reflect sunlight, so less heat reaches the room below.
The fluid inside air conditioners and fridges that carries heat away. Many common ones are powerful greenhouse gases if they leak.
Soot from diesel, wood, coal and brick kilns. It warms the air, and when it settles on snow and ice it darkens them so they melt faster.
A harm that feeds itself: each turn of the loop makes the next one worse. This map shows where those loops could be interrupted.
A response to heat that makes things worse elsewhere or later, such as air conditioners that cool a room but heat the street.

The heat your body takes in from the sun and from hot surfaces around it: roads, walls and roofs. In strong sun it shapes how hot you feel more than air temperature does, which is why shade matters so much.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: How hot or cold a person feels. It depends on air temperature, humidity, wind, sun, clothing and activity, not on air temperature alone.
How much sunlight a surface reflects. A white roof has a high albedo and stays cooler; dark asphalt has a low albedo and stores heat.
Water evaporating from soil and leaves. It draws heat out of the air, so well-watered plants cool their surroundings. Plants short of water stop cooling.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: Using living systems such as trees, wetlands, soils and water to tackle problems like heat and flooding while also benefiting people and nature. A park only works as one if it is planned for those benefits and kept alive.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: The benefits people get from nature: shade and cooling, cleaner air and water, rain soaking into the ground, food and places to rest. The same service is worth most to those with the fewest alternatives, such as cooling for people without air conditioning.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: A network of water (blue) and plants and soil (green), such as rivers, ponds, wetlands, parks and planted drains, designed to manage rain and heat together.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: Engineered, mostly concrete systems such as pipes, drains, embankments and pumps. Many good solutions mix grey and green.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: A city designed to soak up, store, clean and slowly release rainwater through parks, wetlands, permeable ground and planted drains, not only pipes. China piloted it in 30 cities from 2014 to 2019; Chennai and Bangkok are building sponge parks.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: The extra gains a measure brings beyond its main aim, such as a park built to hold floodwater that also cools the street and gives children somewhere to play.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: Using nature to help people adapt to climate change, such as mangroves against storm surges or trees for shade. A kind of nature-based solution.
When a new park or greening raises rents and land prices so much that the poorer residents it was meant to help are pushed out.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: A fair share of environmental benefits and harms, and a fair say in decisions about them. Poorer neighbourhoods are often hotter and less green.

source.label: Nature-Based Solutions for Cities (Edward Elgar, 2023, open access)

text: Underground layers of rock or sand that hold groundwater, the water that wells and pumps draw from.
Growing trees alongside crops or livestock. The trees shade the soil, help it hold moisture and give farmers another source of income.
A city official whose job is heat: joining up health, water, power, schools and work so that protection is planned before the hot season. Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first in 2023.

source.label: One Billion Resilient, 2023

text: Graded warnings, such as caution, danger and extreme danger, set at levels of heat that harm health locally. A good plan ties each level to named actions, so a warning switches protection on.

source.label: WHO/Europe: Heat–health action plans, guidance, second edition, 2026

text: Building shaded rest into each hour of hot, heavy work. In Singapore, employers must give at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy outdoor work at a wet-bulb globe temperature of 32 °C or more.

source.label: Ministry of Manpower, Singapore: enhanced measures to reduce heat stress, 2023

text: A heat action plan that maps risk neighbourhood by neighbourhood, using felt heat, warm nights and who lives there, so help goes first where risk is highest. Thane, next to Mumbai, built its 2024 plan this way.

source.label: CEEW: How can Thane city tackle heatwave risks with a heat action plan

term: Core elements of a heat plan
text: WHO/Europe’s checklist for a complete heat–health action plan: governance, a warning system, people at risk, communication, a resilient health system, reducing exposure, surveillance, and monitoring and learning.

source.label: WHO/Europe: Heat–health action plans, guidance, second edition, 2026

text: Working out how much climate change has added to an event or its harm. The 2026 Lancet Countdown attributes 71.5% of 2023’s heat deaths to climate change, and 11.3 of 13.5 heatwave days per person in 2025.

source.label: The 2026 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change

text: Heat deaths that are never recorded as heat deaths, because certificates name the immediate cause, such as a heart attack. In India in 2024, 185 heatstroke deaths were confirmed against 48,385 suspected heatstroke cases, up to 28 July.

source.label: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, reply in India’s Rajya Sabha, 6 August 2024

text: Work that heat makes unsafe or impossible. The 2026 Lancet Countdown estimates 573 billion potential work hours were lost to heat in 2025, with farm workers losing twice as many hours as any other sector.

source.label: The 2026 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change

text: Work without a formal contract, sick pay or social insurance, often outdoors: street vending, construction, farm and home-based work. An OECD report estimates heat costs informal workers about 2.4% of working hours, against 1.4% for formal workers.

source.label: The Policy Edge, summarising the OECD Development Centre, 2026

text: Lost schooling when heat closes schools or makes classrooms too hot to learn in. In April 2024, Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children, and 5,288 schools in the Philippines moved to remote learning.

source.label: NBC News, 2024; Malay Mail (AFP), 2024

text: The difference between people who can stay cool and those who can’t. Air conditioning may have prevented about 360,000 deaths a year in 2022 and 2023, but only about 3% of households in the poorest countries have it.

source.label: The 2026 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change

text: How much cooling people need, and the energy it takes. Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could rise from about 40 million to 300 million by 2040, half of them in Indonesia.

source.label: International Energy Agency: The Future of Cooling in Southeast Asia

text: The highest electricity load of the day or year, which in hot countries comes with heat and air conditioning. In May and June 2023, heat drove demand up in northern Viet Nam as hydropower reservoirs ran low; blackouts cost about US$1.4 billion.

source.label: The Manila Times, reporting the World Bank, 2023

text: Mountain ice shrinking faster than snow can replace it. In the Hindu Kush Himalaya, glaciers lost ice 65% faster in the 2010s than in the decade before, and could lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100.

source.label: ICIMOD: Water, ice, society and ecosystems in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, 2023

text: Fires that smoulder in drained peatland, the thick, wet soil of tropical swamps. Once dry, peat burns underground for weeks and fills the air with haze. Indonesia’s 2015 forest and peat fires cost an estimated US$16.1 billion.

source.label: World Bank: The cost of fire, Indonesia, 2016

text: Crops need cool nights too. At the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, rice yields fell about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature.

source.label: Peng et al., PNAS, 2004

text: The difference between what countries say they need to adapt to climate change and the money that arrives. Forty-eight countries put their health adaptation needs at about US$3.3 billion a year; international funding committed in 2024 covered about a third.

source.label: The 2026 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change

text: How heat travels from wages to lenders: lost working hours mean missed repayments, and lenders face a cash crunch. About 60% of India’s ₹3.81 trillion microfinance portfolio is in farming and allied work.

source.label: Mongabay India commentary, June 2026

text: With age, thirst fades and the body sweats less, so it cools more slowly and the heart works harder. Older people in a Kolkata informal settlement were 4.3 times more likely than those in a nearby village to face dangerous heat, because their homes stayed hot at night.

source.label: Weitz, Mukhopadhyay and Das, International Journal of Biometeorology, 2022

text: A pregnant body runs warm and has less room to cool. Each 1 °C rise raises the odds of a preterm birth by about 5%, and a heatwave by about 16%.

source.label: Chersich et al., BMJ, 2020

term: Babies and young children in heat
match: babies and young children in heat
text: Babies and small children overheat and lose water faster than adults, and depend on someone else to notice. In 2014–2023, each infant in India faced an average of 7.7 heatwave days a year, 47% more than in the 1990s.

source.label: Lancet Countdown, India data sheet, 2024

text: Sweating and dehydration make the heart work harder and can damage the kidneys, especially with repeated exposure. People already living with heart, kidney or lung conditions have less room to cope.

source.label: Kidney International Reports, 2023

text: To fall asleep, the body needs to cool. On hot nights sleep comes later and ends sooner, so the next day starts already depleted. A study of 47,628 people’s sleep wristbands in 68 countries found hot nights cut sleep.

source.label: Minor et al., One Earth, 2022

text: Heat is linked to more anxiety, distress and suicide, and to worse outcomes for people living with mental illness.

source.label: Thompson et al., The Lancet Planetary Health, 2023, summarised by Imperial College London

term: When home is hotter than outside
match: when home is hotter than outside
text: Thin metal roofs, small windows and crowded rooms can make a home hotter inside than out, worst at night. In Ahmedabad, people in informal settlements faced temperatures up to 7.6 °C higher than people in formal housing.

source.label: Mahadevia et al., 2020, reported in Frontiers in Built Environment, 2022

text: Cooking over a fire in a small, smoky kitchen during a heatwave: a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes.

source.label: Ghimire and others, Frontiers in Public Health, 2025

text: Heatstroke is an emergency, and cooling buys time: move the person to shade, cool them with water and fanning, call for help, and give small sips of water only if they are awake. Hot skin with confusion can mean heatstroke.

source.label: National Centre for Disease Control, India: heat-related illnesses

text: A call or a knock for people who live alone or can’t easily leave home. In Chicago’s 1995 heatwave, living alone and not leaving home were among the strongest risks of dying.

source.label: Semenza et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 1996

text: Prisons, hostels, care homes and crowded shelters, where people can’t leave for shade. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy names prisoners among the groups it is meant to reach, and proposes cool roofs and trees for its jails.

source.label: Tamil Nadu Heat Mitigation Strategy, 2024

text: Heatwaves bring surges of patients just as staff, power and supplies are under strain. In 2024, Indian hospitals prepared heatstroke rooms, ice baths and cooled beds before the peak.

source.label: Context (Thomson Reuters Foundation), 2024

text: A heat warning that reaches clinics a day or two early, so they can add staff, stock fluids and clear beds. After Ahmedabad’s plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an evaluation estimated about 1,190 deaths a year were avoided.

source.label: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018

text: Every fridge and cool box from the factory to the patient or the plate. Without reliable power, fridges for food, medicines and vaccines fail; 526 million tonnes of food are lost each year for lack of refrigeration.

source.label: UNEP and FAO, Sustainable Food Cold Chains, 2022

text: Phone masts and networks need power and cooling too. In Bangladesh in 2026, mobile signals weakened as blackouts spread; warnings, mobile payments and calls for help all ride on them.

source.label: Asia News Network, 2026

text: Demand peaks as everyone switches on cooling, just as hot lines and transformers struggle. An early World Bank estimate put the cost of northern Viet Nam’s power cuts in May and June 2023 at US$1.4 billion.

source.label: World Bank estimate, reported by AFP via The Manila Times, 2023

term: Water for power, power for water
match: water for power, power for water
text: Many power plants need water to cool, and water pumps need power to run, so in a heatwave each strains the other. In 2016, India lost 14 TWh of electricity because thermal power plants ran short of water.

source.label: World Resources Institute, 2018

text: When the grid fails, homes, shops and hospitals that can afford it switch to diesel generators, which keep the lights on and add to the heat and the smoke. There are 20 to 30 million back-up generator sites in low- and middle-income countries.

source.label: IFC, The Dirty Footprint of the Broken Grid, 2019

text: Heat, drought and missing upkeep can kill street trees just when their shade is needed. Across 164 cities, 56% of urban tree and shrub species already face temperatures beyond their natural range, and 76% could by 2050.

source.label: Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022

text: Trees and parks cluster in better-off neighbourhoods, which can pay for them and their upkeep, so poorer districts stay hotter. In Jakarta, green space is concentrated in wealthier areas while dense low-income neighbourhoods act as heat islands.

source.label: Wolch, Byrne and Newell, Landscape and Urban Planning, 2014

text: A hot classroom is hard to learn in, and when it becomes unsafe, schools close. In 2024, heatwaves disrupted the schooling of 171 million students; South Asia was the most affected region.

source.label: UNICEF, Learning interrupted, 2025

term: Roads and rails in the heat
match: roads and rails in the heat
text: Steel rails expand and can buckle, so trains slow; roads soften; hot, thin air means planes need longer runways. Journeys, shifts and supplies, including medicines and food, are delayed.

source.label: Network Rail: buckled rails in summer heat

term: When dry soil heats the air
match: when dry soil heats the air
text: Moist soil cools the air as its water evaporates. When soil dries, that cooling stops, so the air heats faster and dries the soil further: a loop that water kept in the ground can break.

source.label: Seneviratne et al., Earth-Science Reviews, 2010

text: On Puncak Jaya in Papua, Indonesia, 99% of the glacier area has gone since 1850. About 0.17 km² was left in 2024, and it will very likely disappear around 2030.

source.label: Ibel, Mölg and Sommer, The Cryosphere, 2025

text: Heat and drought lower rivers and canals, and the sea pushes inland. In Viet Nam’s Mekong Delta in February 2024, farmers who pumped salty canal water onto their rice lost up to half their crop.

source.label: Viet Nam News, 2024
